title: Joint Injection Pathways: Corticosteroid Injection for Osteoarthritis

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee, hip or a smaller joint in a Saudi primary care, rheumatology or orthopaedic clinic: when an intra-articular corticosteroid injection is appropriate, what to do first, who should not have it, how to prepare and inject, aftercare, repeat injections, and what to tell the patient. Uses NICE NG226 and a systematic review of international guidelines with the Depo-Medrol, Kenalog-10 and Xylocaine product labels and a Saudi survey of patient misconceptions; no Saudi national guideline on joint injection was found.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-14.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health, Saudi Society for Rheumatology or Saudi Orthopaedic guideline on intra-articular corticosteroid injection was found; NICE NG226 (United Kingdom, 2022) is the main guideline. The American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation 2019 guideline is quoted only through the Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review of guidelines and was not read directly.

Guidelines disagree on corticosteroid injection: the review found it recommended with caution overall; the American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends it for knee and hip, the European League Against Rheumatism recommends it for flares with effusion, OARSI and the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners give a conditional recommendation, and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons made no recommendation (2013).

A single starting dose for the knee is a clinical choice: the Depo-Medrol label gives 20 to 80 mg for large joints (knee, ankle, shoulder), 10 to 40 mg for medium joints and 4 to 10 mg for small joints, and the Kenalog-10 label gives 5 to 15 mg for larger joints; no source read gives an optimal dose for knee osteoarthritis.

How many injections are safe per year and the minimum interval were not found: the Depo-Medrol label says injections may be repeated at 1 to 5 or more weeks depending on relief, the review warns that repeated injections can cause harm, and NICE gives only 2 to 10 weeks of relief; no interval is written beyond these statements.

Local anaesthetic volume: the Kenalog-10 label says prior local anaesthetic may be desirable and the Depo-Medrol label says infiltration is elective; the volume of lidocaine at the skin is a clinical choice. The Xylocaine label warns of chondrolysis after intra-articular infusion of local anaesthetics and states it is not approved for this use, so lidocaine is written for the skin and tissue track only, not into the joint.
Image guidance with ultrasound or fluoroscopy, hip injection technique and the effect on diabetic glucose control are not detailed; no source with a regimen was read for them.
Hyaluronic acid, platelet-rich plasma and glucosamine are not written as regimens because NICE advises against hyaluronan and glucosamine and the review found platelet-rich plasma not recommended.

Topical and oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are first-line medicines in NICE NG226 but no label was reviewed for this topic, so no regimen is written; see the knee and hip osteoarthritis topics for those.
The Saudi survey is a convenience sample of 405 adults and shows beliefs, not clinical outcomes.
Figures were read by automated extraction of web and label text; spot-check each dose against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Osteoarthritis is a whole-joint disease with cartilage loss, bone change and synovial inflammation; a steroid injection reduces synovitis and pain for a short time but does not change the disease (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.10; Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A). Pain relief from an intra-articular steroid lasts 2 to 10 weeks and in trials may be under 4 weeks (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.10; Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review, Section Discussion). A steroid injected into an infected joint can make the infection worse, so septic arthritis must be excluded first (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings). Repeated steroid injection may harm cartilage and joint tissue and cause aseptic necrosis, calcinosis and Charcot-like arthropathy (Kenalog-10 label, Adverse Reactions; Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review, Section Corticosteroid Injections). Part of the injected dose is absorbed into the blood, which can raise glucose and suppress the immune system (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings). Treatment failure is most often because the needle did not enter the joint space; little benefit follows injection into the surrounding tissue (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A).

symptoms: Activity-related joint pain that is not controlled by exercise, weight management and topical or oral medicines (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.1.1 and Recommendation 1.4.10).
Acute flare of knee pain, especially with an effusion (Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review, Section Corticosteroid Injections).
Morning stiffness lasting no longer than 30 minutes (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.1.1).
Wish to delay surgery or to support exercise; in a Saudi survey 83.9% of those injected gave delaying surgery as the reason (Saudi survey of misconceptions, Results).
physicalSigns: Bony enlargement, crepitus, reduced movement and joint-line tenderness (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.1.1).
Effusion of the knee (Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review, Section Corticosteroid Injections).
Warm, red, markedly swollen joint with fever suggests septic arthritis: do not inject (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Skin infection or broken skin over the planned needle track (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
redFlags: Hot, swollen painful joint with fever or inability to bear weight: exclude septic arthritis by joint aspiration before any steroid (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Marked increase in pain with swelling, loss of movement, fever and malaise after injection: suspect septic arthritis and refer urgently (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Acute local infection at the injection site or a previously infected joint: do not inject (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Anaphylaxis or severe allergic reaction after injection: manage as an emergency (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).

Patient on anticoagulants, with a bleeding disorder or idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura: check before injecting; intramuscular corticosteroid preparations are contraindicated in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
Do not inject into the spine, sacroiliac joints, epidural space or intravenously (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A; Kenalog-10 label, Warnings).
precipitants: Diabetes: glucose rises for several days (Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions).
Recent or repeated steroid injections into the same joint (Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review, Section Corticosteroid Injections).
Immunosuppression or infection elsewhere (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Hepatitis B carrier status: reactivation can occur with immunosuppressive doses (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Injection leakage into the skin can cause atrophy (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Hot, red, very painful joint with fever; joint fluid shows infection (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Acute, severe onset of a single hot joint; crystals in joint fluid (Depo-Medrol label, Indications B).

differentials.condition: Inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Morning stiffness longer than 30 minutes and multiple joints (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.1.1).

differentials.condition: Referred or soft tissue pain (bursitis, tendinopathy)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pain localised to a bursa or tendon rather than the joint line (Depo-Medrol label, Indications B).
Night or rest pain with atypical features; imaging is needed (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.1.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Diagnose and assess
actions: Diagnose osteoarthritis clinically in people aged 45 or over with activity-related pain and short morning stiffness; image only if atypical (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.1.1 and Recommendation 1.1.2).
Explain that exercise and weight management are the core treatments and give information and support (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.2.2).
Look for hot, swollen joint, fever or other signs of infection (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).

clinicalManagement.title: Use first-line treatments first
actions: Offer tailored therapeutic exercise and weight loss if overweight (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.3.1 and Recommendation 1.3.5).

Offer a topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for knee osteoarthritis, and consider an oral one with gastroprotection if topical treatment fails (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.2 and Recommendation 1.4.4).
Do not offer glucosamine or strong opioids (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.6).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide on injection with the patient
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When other treatments are not enough
actions: Consider an intra-articular corticosteroid injection when other pharmacological treatments are ineffective or unsuitable, or to support exercise (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.10).

Explain benefit of 2 to 10 weeks, the risk of infection, flare and joint damage with repeated injections, and that it is not a cure (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.10; Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A).
Address myths: in a Saudi survey 48.4% had never heard of intra-articular injections and 16.1% held misconceptions such as that it liquefies bone (Saudi survey of misconceptions, Results).
Obtain and record consent (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.2.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Check for reasons not to inject
actions: Confirm no infection at the site or in the joint, no allergy, and review diabetes, anticoagulants and live vaccines (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications and Warnings).
Aspirate and examine the fluid if septic arthritis is possible (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).

clinicalManagement.title: Inject into the joint space
actions: Review the anatomy and use strict aseptic technique; clean the vial top and use a sterile 20 to 24 gauge needle on a dry syringe (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A; Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration).

Enter the synovial space where it is most superficial and free of large vessels; aspiration of a few drops of fluid shows the joint space has been entered (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A).
Aspirate excess fluid if there is a large effusion, then inject the shaken suspension without delay (Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration).
Avoid leakage into the skin or surrounding tissue because this can cause atrophy (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings; Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration).

clinicalManagement.title: Aftercare
actions: Give the patient written advice on warning signs of infection and when to seek care (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Encourage regular exercise to build on the benefit (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.10).
Tell people with diabetes to check glucose more often for several days (Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions).

clinicalManagement.title: Review and plan repeat treatment
actions: Use patient-initiated follow-up for most people and planned follow-up when needed (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.5.1 and Recommendation 1.5.2).

Take care with repeated injections because of potential harm; consider referral for joint replacement if symptoms persist (Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review, Section Corticosteroid Injections; NICE NG226, Section 1.6).

regimens.indication: Short-term relief of pain and synovitis in osteoarthritis of a joint
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with osteoarthritis not controlled by other treatments
regimens.dose: Large joint (knee, ankle, shoulder): 20 to 80 mg; medium joint (elbow, wrist): 10 to 40 mg; small joint (finger joints): 4 to 10 mg, as a general guide (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A.1). Use the lowest effective dose. Dilution and preparation: do not dilute or mix with other solutions because of possible physical incompatibility; shake the vial; clean the vial top with povidone-iodine before aspirating; use strict aseptic technique (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration and Precautions).
regimens.route: Intra-articular injection into the synovial space with a sterile 20 to 24 gauge needle on a dry syringe after aspiration of a few drops of joint fluid; not for intravenous, intrathecal or epidural use; do not inject into surrounding tissue (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A)
regimens.frequency: Single injection; the label says injections may be repeated at intervals of one to five or more weeks depending on relief, but repeated injections may harm joint tissue (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration A.1; Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021 review, Section Corticosteroid Injections)
regimens.duration: Relief lasts about 2 to 10 weeks (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.10)
adjustments: Contains benzyl alcohol as a preservative; contraindicated in premature infants (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
Diabetes: glucose rises for days and antidiabetic doses may need adjustment (Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions).
Hepatitis B carriers may have reactivation at immunosuppressive doses (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Live vaccines are contraindicated at immunosuppressive doses (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
CYP3A4 inducers can reduce the effect (Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Signs of joint infection: marked increase in pain, swelling, fever, malaise (Depo-Medrol label, Precautions).
Post-injection flare in the first day or two (Depo-Medrol label, Adverse Reactions).
Blood glucose in diabetes for several days (Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions).
Skin atrophy or depigmentation at the site (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to the product or its constituents (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura for intramuscular preparations (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
Acute local infection at the site; previously infected joint is not usually injected (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings and Precautions).
Systemic fungal infection, except an intra-articular injection for a localised joint condition (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
regimens.useWhen: Preferred: label gives dose ranges for large, medium and small joints and covers osteoarthritis.

regimens.indication: Short-term relief of pain and synovitis in osteoarthritis of a joint
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with osteoarthritis not controlled by other treatments
regimens.dose: 2.5 to 5 mg for a smaller joint and 5 to 15 mg for a larger joint (Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration: Intra-Articular Administration). Dilution and preparation: use the 10 mg per mL suspension as supplied; shake the vial; inspect for clumping and discard if agglomerated; inject without delay so it does not settle in the syringe (Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration: Administration).
regimens.route: Intra-articular injection only, using the usual joint technique and strict aseptic technique; if excess synovial fluid is present remove some but not all; not for intravenous, intramuscular, intraocular, epidural or intrathecal use (Kenalog-10 label, boxed statement and Dosage and Administration)
regimens.frequency: Single injection; injections into several joints up to a total of 20 mg or more have been given (Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration)
regimens.duration: Relief lasts about 2 to 10 weeks (NICE NG226, Recommendation 1.4.10)
adjustments: The 10 mg per mL strength is suitable for intra-articular and intralesional use only (Kenalog-10 label, Description).
Contains benzyl alcohol 0.99%; avoid in neonates (Kenalog-10 label, Warnings).
Avoid injecting into surrounding tissue, particularly the deltoid region, because of tissue atrophy (Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration).
Intra-articular injection may damage joint tissue (Kenalog-10 label, Precautions).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Signs of joint infection or flare after injection (Kenalog-10 label, Precautions).
Blood glucose in diabetes (Kenalog-10 label, Drug Interactions).
Skin atrophy at the site (Kenalog-10 label, Dosage and Administration).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to any component (Kenalog-10 label, Contraindications).
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura for intramuscular preparations (Kenalog-10 label, Contraindications).
Epidural, intrathecal, intravenous, intramuscular or intraocular administration (Kenalog-10 label, Warnings).
Acute local infection at the site (Kenalog-10 label, Precautions).
regimens.useWhen: Choose when methylprednisolone acetate is unavailable or the unit protocol prefers triamcinolone acetonide for smaller doses.

regimens.indication: Numbing of the skin and needle track before intra-articular injection (optional)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults having a joint injection who want pain relief at the needle site
regimens.dose: Small volume of 1% lidocaine (for example 1 to 2 mL, 10 to 20 mg) at the skin and tissue along the needle track; the volume is a clinical choice and the label advises the lowest dose that gives effective anaesthesia (Xylocaine label, Dosage and Administration). Dilution and preparation: none; use the 1% solution as supplied; only methylparaben-free single-dose vials should be used near the joint (Xylocaine label, Warnings).
regimens.route: Local infiltration of the skin and subcutaneous tissue at the needle site, aspirating before injection to avoid intravascular injection; do not infuse into the joint because of reported chondrolysis after intra-articular infusion of local anaesthetics (Xylocaine label, Warnings and Dosage and Administration)
adjustments: Use caution in severe liver disease (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Methaemoglobinaemia risk with oxidising drugs (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Do not exceed the label maximum dose; the lowest dose that gives effective anaesthesia should be used (Xylocaine label, Dosage and Administration).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Signs of systemic toxicity: perioral numbness, dizziness, tinnitus, convulsions (Xylocaine label, Adverse Reactions).
Allergic reactions including to methylparaben in multiple-dose vials (Xylocaine label, Adverse Reactions).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anaesthetics (Xylocaine label, Contraindications).

teaching.scope: Adult with symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee, hip or a smaller joint in a Saudi primary care, rheumatology or orthopaedic clinic: when an intra-articular corticosteroid injection is appropriate, what to do first, who should not have it, how to prepare and inject, aftercare, repeat injections, and what to tell the patient. learningObjectives: Diagnose osteoarthritis clinically and start with exercise, weight management and topical or oral medicines.
Consider a corticosteroid injection when these are not enough, and explain relief lasts 2 to 10 weeks.
Exclude infection and check allergy, diabetes, anticoagulants and live vaccines before injecting.

patientEducation: An injection can reduce pain for a few weeks (2 to 10) but does not cure arthritis.
Exercise and weight loss remain the most important treatments.
Expect some soreness for a day or two.
Contact us at once if the joint becomes hot, red, very painful or you develop a fever.
If you have diabetes, check your sugar more often for several days.
Repeated injections into the same joint can damage it, so we will review before another.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep moving with regular tailored exercise.
Lose weight if overweight: 10% is better than 5%.
Use a walking stick for lower limb arthritis if it helps.
Pace activities and rest during flares.
Avoid heavy impact on the injected joint for the first day or two.
mdtReferrals: Family physician or primary care physician; rheumatologist; orthopaedic surgeon; physiotherapist; nurse; pharmacist; dietitian.
dischargeCriteria: Consent recorded; joint, dose and product recorded; aftercare and warning signs given in writing; glucose advice for diabetes; follow-up plan agreed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Patient-initiated follow-up for most people; review at 2 to 10 weeks when relief fades; consider joint replacement referral if symptoms persist despite treatment.
